title: Righteous in his generation (Genesis 6:9)
hook: the rabbis argue whether Noah was great in any age or only beside his neighbors

segments.voice: Yesterday: shomer, a keeper. Cain shrugged off his brother, and the Torah kept answering him: yes.

Ten generations from Adam to Noah, the Mishnah counts, and things have gone badly: the earth, the Torah says, is filled with violence. Then one sentence about one man. Noah was, in his generations, a man righteous and wholehearted. "Noah walked with God." Pure praise? Picture the best student in a class where everyone else stopped showing up. Great, or just great by comparison? The rabbis caught one Hebrew word, bedorotav, in his generations, and started to argue.
screen: `THE EARTH FILLED WITH VIOLENCE.` → `ONE MAN WALKS WITH GOD.` → `IN HIS GENERATIONS?`

segments.voice: Tzaddik: a righteous person. It comes from tzedek, justice, rightness, things set straight, the same root as tzedakah, the giving you met on day sixteen. Now the argument. The Talmud records two teachers, Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, reading the phrase in opposite ways. One says it's criticism: he was righteous only compared to them; in Abraham's day, nobody would have noticed him. The other says it's praise: if he stayed good in a generation like that, with no one to learn from, imagine him among good people. Rashi, the great medieval commentator, sets both readings side by side and doesn't pick. The tradition keeps both, because both are true of people. Some are good because everyone around them is. Some are good in spite of everyone around them. And from the inside, it's hard to know which one you are. Another small detail. Noah walked with God; later, Abraham speaks of the God before whom he walks. Rashi says Noah needed God beside him to hold him up, while Abraham could walk ahead on his own. Not an insult: an honest picture of a man doing his best. And the Talmud says every generation has at least thirty-six righteous people. Later folk tradition made them hidden, unknown even to themselves: tzaddikim nobody would ever put in a book.
screen: `TZEDEK — JUSTICE, RIGHTNESS.` · `CRITICISM OR PRAISE?` · `RASHI KEEPS BOTH READINGS.` · `THIRTY-SIX HIDDEN RIGHTEOUS.` · then, large: `NOAH WALKED WITH GOD.`

segments.voice: Think of the people around you this week, at work, at home, online, and how much they shape what you do. Then hold in mind one right thing you could do that nobody will see: returning something, fixing what someone else broke, a kind word about someone who isn't there. If you pray, you can ask for the strength to be good where you are.
Tzaddik. A righteous person, from tzedek, justice. Genesis gives the word to Noah.
Your line: good where you are. Not better than the room, just right in the room you're in. That's day thirty-two.

howItsDone: Jews read the story of Noah each autumn as the weekly Torah portion Noach, and the rabbinic argument over "in his generations" is a favorite text for study and sermons that week.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: "ten generations" now credited to the Mishnah (Avot 5:2); "three little words" fixed to one Hebrew word, bedorotav; the tzedakah-is-justice teaching cut to a callback (day 10 taught it); Rashi's contrast now matches his source (Abraham's own words, Genesis 24:40); the thirty-six split into what the Talmud says and what later folklore adds; "the first person the Torah calls one" softened.
Genesis 6:9 in JPS 1917 reads roughly 'Noah was in his generations a man righteous and whole-hearted'; only 'Noah walked with God' is quoted. The rest is paraphrased in the hook. Confirm.
Sanhedrin 108a: confirm which of Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish holds which reading (commonly: R. Yochanan criticism, Resh Lakish praise). The script deliberately doesn't assign them.
Rashi on 6:9 contrasting 'walked with God' (needing support) and Abraham's 'walk before Me' (Genesis 17:1; Rashi there/Genesis Rabbah 30:10): confirm.
The thirty-six hidden righteous (lamed-vav tzaddikim) derive from Sanhedrin 97b / Sukkah 45b; 'unknown even to themselves' is from later folk tradition. Confirm phrasing.
Claim that Noah is the first person the Torah calls tzaddik: confirm.
